findings.description: In a blockquote, when a `<pre` tag spans more than one line, the `>` marker at the start of the next line ends the tag in `PRE_TAG`. GitHub removes that marker before parsing the HTML, so the `lang="suggestion"` after it is posted unchanged.
findings.body:
**A blockquote's `>` marker ends the tag early for `PRE_TAG`, but not for GitHub** `PRE_TAG` and `TAG_ATTRIBUTE` treat any `>` outside a quoted value as the end of the tag. On a continuation line in a blockquote, markdown removes the `> ` marker before the HTML reaches the parser: ```ts const PRE_TAG = /])(?:[\s/]+|[^\s/>][^\s/>=]*(?:\s*=\s*(?:"[^"]*"?|'[^']*'?|[^\s>]*))?)*/gi; const TAG_ATTRIBUTE = /[\s/]+|([^\s/>][^\s/>=]*)(?:\s*=\s*("[^"]*"?|'[^']*'?|[^\s>]*))?/g; ``` https://github.com/AlexisBalayre/claude-code-config/blob/799fa4868ee037b7e7c97d6988bcf43ea516acdb/tools/review/src/review-body.utils.ts#L28-L29 Input: ``` > 
 lang="suggestion">evil();
``` `PRE_TAG` matches ``. `lang="suggestion"` is never scanned, and the output equals the input. cmark-gfm opens a type-1 HTML block in the quote (`evil();`. At 30f8210 the scoped scan ran to ` 
 lang=suggestion>` gets past both. (Renderer behaviour, so confidence is medium.)

Fix direction: in both regexes, count a line break followed by blockquote markers (`\r?\n(?:[^\S\r\n]*>)*`) as whitespace. It has to come before the generic `[\s/]+` alternative and also go inside the `\s*=\s*` separator. The cost is that a real `` outside a blockquote makes the scan read into the next line, which can only over-rewrite. Please add the input above as a test row.

findings.description: JavaScript's `\s` matches characters HTML does not count as whitespace (U+00A0, U+000B, U+FEFF, U+2000-U+200A, U+3000 and others). HTML whitespace is only tab, LF, FF, CR and space. In `\s*=\s*`, `\s` accepts NBSP before a quoted value where HTML starts an unquoted value instead, so the regex opens a quote HTML never opens.
findings.body:
**JS `\s` is wider than HTML whitespace, so the regex opens a quote HTML never opens** `PRE_TAG` and `TAG_ATTRIBUTE` use `\s` wherever the HTML tokenizer skips whitespace. JS `\s` also covers U+00A0, U+000B, U+FEFF, U+2000–U+200A, U+3000 and others. HTML whitespace is only tab, LF, FF, CR (normalised to LF) and space. https://github.com/AlexisBalayre/claude-code-config/blob/799fa4868ee037b7e7c97d6988bcf43ea516acdb/tools/review/src/review-body.utils.ts#L28-L29 Input (with ` ` written as NBSP): `
evil();
` - **HTML5:** after `=`, NBSP is not whitespace, so it starts the unquoted value ` "x`, which ends at the space. `lang=suggestion` is a real attribute, `"` becomes a junk attribute name, and `>` closes the tag. - **Regex:** `\s*=\s*` takes the NBSP, then `"[^"]*"?` reads `"x lang=suggestion "` as a single quoted value. `TAG_ATTRIBUTE` sees only `a`, so `lang` is posted unchanged. The end of an unquoted value (`[^\s>]*`) fails the same way: `
`. A NBSP that `\s` treats as a break between names only over-rewrites, which is harmless. At 30f8210 the `\blang\s*=` scan caught both inputs. cmark-gfm opens the type-1 HTML block without checking attribute syntax, so the bytes reach the sanitizer unchanged. Whether `lang` survives there rests on this module's own premise, so confidence is medium.

Use HTML's whitespace set in both regexes, and add the input above as a test row.

findings.description: `PRE_TAG` and `TAG_ATTRIBUTE` each spell out the same attribute grammar (the name class, the `\s*=\s*` separator, the three value forms), and they must stay in lockstep. If one gains a form the other lacks, `PRE_TAG` ends the tag at a different point from where `TAG_ATTRIBUTE` tokenizes it. Building both from shared source fragments with `new RegExp` would remove the drift risk.

`tag.slice(0, 4)` / `.slice(4)` hard-code the length of `<pre`, which the regex only implies. Capturing `(<pre)` in `PRE_TAG` and reusing it in the replacer, or running a sticky `TAG_ATTRIBUTE` from `lastIndex = 4`, would remove the coupling.

The footnote-label linear-time test asserts with wall-clock time (`toBeLessThan(100)`), which can flake on a loaded CI runner. The margin is wide (2^28 steps against microseconds), so the risk is low. A one-line WHY naming the exponential-backtracking regression it guards would make a failure easier to read.
